title: The Lucena position: the bridge
summary: Rook and pawn against rook: the position that wins, and the bridge that takes the pawn to a queen.
part.lucena.title: The Lucena position
part.lucena.summary: The winning position, why the king cannot just step aside, and the two preparatory moves.
part.bridge.title: The bridge
part.bridge.summary: The king steps out, withstands the checks and the rook closes the bridge; and why the fourth rank is the safe one.
part.defenses.title: Defences, the way in and recap
part.defenses.summary: The black rook on the fourth rank, how to reach the Lucena, the short-side exception, and the rules.
step.key: This is the Lucena position. Keep the picture: the pawn on the seventh, your king in front of it on the queening square; the black rook holds your king from the side, and your rook cuts the black king off by at least one file. With any pawn but a rook pawn, this is a win. Karsten Müller says it may be the most important position in all of endgame theory.
step.stuck: The problem is getting out from in front of the pawn. If the king goes to c7, the black rook checks on c2; king b6, check on b2; king a7, check on a2. The rook returns and the king returns with it. We need shelter from the checks. That is what the bridge is for.
step.push: Two preparatory moves. First, drive the black king one more file away, with check. Then lift the rook to the fourth rank: it is going to be the bridge.
step.push.hint: A rook check on the d-file pushes the king away; then the rook goes up to d4.
step.push.done: That's it. The black king is two files from the pawn and the rook waits on the fourth rank. Now your king can come out.
step.bridge: Black waits. Now the king comes out and takes the checks: it walks down the c- and b-files, always next to the pawn, until it reaches the fifth rank. When the check comes on b1, the rook steps in on b4: the bridge is built.
step.bridge.hint: The king goes c7, b6, c6, b5, always next to the pawn. On the fifth rank, the rook blocks the check on b4.
step.bridge.done: The bridge. The black rook has no more checks, and nothing is left to hold the pawn.
step.bridgeDone: Look at what Black has left: if the rook takes on b4, the king recaptures and the pawn queens. If it does not take, the pawn queens anyway. The name comes from Nimzowitsch, in My System, 1925: the rook is the bridge under which the king crosses.
step.whyFourth: Why the fourth rank, and not the fifth? Because the black king comes closer. Here it stands on e6: the rook on d4 is out of its reach. If I played Rd5 now, it would be a serious mistake: the black rook takes the pawn on b7, the king recaptures and the rook on d5 falls. A draw. The fourth rank is the safe shelter.
step.trap: So how do we solve it? A check on the sixth rank, to drive the black king away, and only then the rook goes to the fifth. The rest is the same: king to b6, and the rook closes on b5, the bridge one rank higher.
step.trap.hint: First the check on d6, pushing the king to the seventh. Then Rd5, king b6, and the rook blocks on b5.
step.trap.done: Well done. The bridge works on the fifth rank too, as long as the black king cannot reach the rook.
step.rook4: A clever defence: the black rook sits on the fourth rank and forbids your rook from going up to d4. No harm done. The king comes out right away, via c7, and answers the checks with b6 and a6. The black rook is too close and the checks run out quickly. Then the white rook goes to d5 and closes on b5: the bridge on the fifth.
step.reach: Now from a little further away. Your king is already on the queening square and the pawn on the sixth. Push the pawn to the seventh: it is the Lucena. Since the black king is already two files away, the rook can go straight to the fourth rank.
step.reach.hint: b7 takes the pawn to the seventh with the king in front. Then the rook goes up to c4.
step.reach.done: There. Did you recognise the position? The rest is the bridge you already know.
step.shortSide: Now the other side of the board. Not every position that looks like this is a win. Here Black is to move, the black rook is far away on the long side of the pawn, and the black king stands on the short side, out of the way. Ra8+, Ra7+, Ra6+: the white king has no shelter and cannot approach the rook without leaving the pawn. A draw. At least three files between the rook and the king: that is the measure. With the pawn, cut the enemy king off on the long side; without it, send your rook far away.
step.finish: Now it is up to you. Pawn on the seventh, king in front, rook cutting off. Drive the black king away, lift the rook, come out with the king and close the bridge. Take the pawn to a queen.
step.recap: Three rules to take with you. One: king in front of the pawn on the queening square, enemy king cut off, is the Lucena, and it wins with every pawn but a rook pawn. Two: check to drive the king away, rook to the fourth rank. Three: the king comes out, walks to the fifth rank next to the pawn, and the rook closes the bridge. Bridge closed, game over.
step.t_lucena: Pawn on the seventh, your king in front of it, the black king cut off by your rook. Before I explain: why can't the king simply step away from the pawn, and what would the plan be?
step.t_lucena.hint1: Watch what the black rook does each time your king steps out. Your own rook could become a shelter.
step.t_rook4: The same Lucena position. This time, look through the defender's eyes: what is Black's most annoying defence, and how do you answer it?
step.t_rook4.hint1: Think about the rank your rook would use for the bridge. Can the black rook get there first?
ex.e12: White to play and win. A king's pawn, and the black rook reached the fourth rank first: there is no bridge there. How does White make progress?
ex.e12.hint: First drive the black king away with a check. Then ask whether your king really needs shelter: the black rook is too close to keep checking for long.
ex.e12.solution: Rc1+ drives the king to b7, and Kd7! walks out at once, with no bridge. The checks soon run out: Rd4+ Ke6, Re4+ Kd6, and the white rook comes back along the d-file (Rd1, Rd5+) to shut the road on the fifth rank. Other moves also win, but walking out with the king is the shortest road: with the black rook so close, the king needs no bridge. Hawkins' line, quoted by Wikipedia.
ex.e13: White to play and win. Andersson vs Åkesson, Skellefteå, 1999. Two pawns against one, but the clearest road goes through a position you already know.
ex.e13.hint: With a single pawn, which position do you want on the board? Look for a pawn trade that leaves the black king cut off.
ex.e13.solution: e4! After dxe4 Rxe4, the black king is cut off by the rook and the f-pawn, with the white king beside it, goes on to the Lucena. The game went 80...Kd7 81.Kg6 and Black resigned. Re6+, Re7 and Re8 also win, but e4 is Andersson's idea: trade into the position you know is won.
ex.e14: White to play and win. The pawn is still on the third rank and the black rook is already attacking it. Take the pawn forward without letting the black king come back.
ex.e14.hint: The pawn advances protected by the king, not by the rook. When the black king comes close, the rook cuts it off along the file.
ex.e14.solution: e4! The king on f5 protects the pawn (Rb7+ also wins). After Kc5, e5 moves on again, and when the black king reaches d5, Rd7+ cuts it off along the d-file. From there it is the known road: pawn on the seventh, king in front, bridge. Defending the pawn with the rook or moving the king away from f5 draws. From Lichess Practice.
ex.e15: White to play and win. A rook's pawn, which nearly always draws. Here there is a chance, and only because White has the move. Find it.
ex.e15.hint: The black king sits next to the b-file and locks your king in the corner. Push it away first; the rook on the fourth rank does the rest.
ex.e15.solution: Rc4+! drives the black king to d7. Then Kb7 leaves the corner, and after the check on b1 the king goes to a6, next to the pawn: with the rook already on the fourth rank, the checks run out and the pawn promotes. With Black to move, Rc1 or Kc7 holds the draw. With a rook's pawn, the Lucena only wins like this: the rook already on the fourth rank and White to move.
ex.e16: White to play and win. Topalov vs Karpov, Cannes, 2002. The black king is right next to the pawn and Black still has the h-pawn. No bridge in sight. What now?
ex.e16.hint: Your rook cannot let go of the h-pawn. Look for the position where Black, having to move, must give something up.
ex.e16.solution: Topalov played Rh7+ Kd8 Rh8+ Kd7 Rh6!: the starting position again, now with Black to move. It is zugzwang: every Black move makes things worse. The h-pawn falls, the king steps away from the pawn, or the rook leaves the a-file and the white king gets out. The game went 72...Kd8 73.Rh7 Rb4 74.Ka7 Ra4+ 75.Kb6 and Karpov resigned. The rook loses a tempo without leaving the h-file: Rh8 on the first move, or Rh6 and Rh5 on the second, also win.
ex.e17: White to play and win. A rook's pawn again, but now the black king is far away. This is Silman's line quoted by Wikipedia, after 1.Rc1 Ke7. Every move counts, right to the end.
ex.e17.hint: The rook goes in front of the pawn, along the b-file, so the king can get out. Then the king walks towards the black king, and at the end there is a sacrifice.
ex.e17.solution: Rc8 and Rb8: the rook on the b-file frees the king. Ra2, and Kb7 steps out; the king escapes the checks via c8 and d8, towards the black king. When the black rook goes to h2, Rb6+ Kc5 and Rc6+!: if Kxc6, a8=Q+ and it is queen against rook, which wins; if the king runs, the rook goes back and the pawn promotes. With a rook's pawn, it only wins with the black king cut off far away.
key.lucena: The Lucena position as Salvio published it in 1634, crediting it to Scipione Genovino. White wins whoever is to move.
key.villa5: The bridge on the fifth rank, a position Wikipedia cites from De la Villa. Rf4 is the safest; Rf5 wins too.
key.rook4: Black to move: the rook goes to the fourth rank and stops the bridge there. White still wins with the bridge on the fifth, in the Emms line cited by Wikipedia.
key.shortSide: The exception: Black to play draws with checks from the side. De la Villa's position 10.4, cited by Wikipedia.
key.practiceBridge: The Lucena on the kingside, from Lichess Practice: Re1+, Re4 and the bridge on g4.
history: The name is a historical mistake. Luis Ramírez de Lucena published in Salamanca, around 1497, the oldest surviving printed chess book, but the position is not in it. The first known publication is by Alessandro Salvio, in Il Puttino, Naples, 1634, and Salvio credits it to Scipione Genovino; a sixteenth-century manuscript, written by a pupil of Genovino, may be older still. The wrong name probably arose in the sixth edition of the Handbuch des Schachspiels, in 1880, which cited a non-existent Lucena 96, and it was repeated by Berger and by Reuben Fine. The phrase building a bridge is Nimzowitsch's, from My System, 1925. Today rook endings occur in eight to ten percent of games, and the Lucena is their key position: Ulf Andersson, against Ralf Åkesson in Skellefteå, 1999, exchanged pawns just to reach it, and his opponent resigned before the bridge ever appeared on the board.
practice: Now the real ending: rook and pawn against rook, with your king far away and the black rook active. Bring the king in front of the pawn, cut the black king off and look for the Lucena. I will be checking the bridge.
